title: Bill Colburn, Morton in California and Finger Buster
summary: Colburn's friendship with Morton, his sales of the album, the Finger Buster story, Morton's illness and will.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: But I'll go over all these jelly notes and I don't think there's anything much more here I wanted to mention about him. Oh there's a little dope here from Bill Colburn and a good friend who liked musicians. When Leadbelly would go out there he'd have him live in his home just to try to learn about the blues when Bunk went out there. He'd known Bunk down here but he invited Bunk to live at his home. Some of that will be in the letters we have written from Bill Colburn's home on Columbus Avenue. Jelly used to go down and see Bill Colburn used to go down to Los Angeles just to see Jelly when he moved to California. Incidentally that album I said wouldn't sell or I had the review because they were going to chase customers out. Bill Colburn had that album he'd go all over town in San Francisco where he lived and play it for everybody and that got to be one of the best sellers in San Francisco. Sherman Clay couldn't keep enough of them there because everybody he'd play it for and he'd talk him into buying it.

Yeah. So Bill would go down to see Jelly when he moved out there. He was already sick and could hardly play. And Bill would start to get Jelly talking. He'd prod him with things like he'd say, well you're alright but you can't play the stuff like Teddy Wilson. Teddy Wilson, I know you're good for that old time stuff but you can't play that new stuff you can't get around on the piano. Or like Art Tatum and all that. So once it got Jelly so burned up that Jelly said I'll play something those guys can't play and even when he was sick he went over to the piano Dink had a piano in his house I guess at that time and played the Finger Buster which nobody knew he'd ever recorded. He'd made a record on the but he said he played all that Finger Buster stuff. Incidentally this somebody was asking me the other day what I thought of Willie the Lion Smith or something and I said I never paid any attention to him. Much around New York used to hear him with Bechet but he brought out a record as if he'd composed it even later than that on Commodore called Finger Buster which is a pretty bad record same tune and all that Jelly I don't know when Jelly went out there he was trying to get up a band with Mutt Carey and all and Mutt had a job in some little I think called Silver Dollar little place down on about 12th Street and Main Street or he was I can't get all this story quite straight but nobody ever heard of Jelly out there for many years he hadn't been there for maybe 30 years or so and the boss wanted him to hire Jelly and told Mutt he better to hire him and all of them so they asked Jelly just who he was they sort of insulted him he said oh you don't know who I am hell you don't read the papers you know poor Jelly's name hadn't been in the papers for years but they thought that he thought everybody should know him I mean he still had that good opinion of himself I were his solos either so anyway he got pretty sick I guess when he was out there soon and wasn't able to play for very long but he actually had hoped to play when he was out there I know Roy Carew told me that even when he was in New York for that last band the one I missed rehearsing that he could tell he was just so ! sick then he would be saving his strength hardly playing with the band at all Roy knew him quite well enough to know whether he was really saving himself or not so he could take a solo chorus at that time they were having solos all the time of course but he must have been quite sick and quite weak out there incidentally I have a copy of his will someplace I haven't seen that I had a photostat made from I probably have just a negative of that which we can copy I don't know where all that material is now it must be here in New Orleans in some box I haven't seen it for many years anybody can go through the probate court files I have a copy it lying on top of the pile I have at home so I'll go through all those material things like that and I can send that will so we can get it photostatted if I don't come across it when I pack and I that Tony Jackson was the greatest pianist and the greatest and all that he'd ever heard but Jelly also knew of course he was good and said but my left hand enabled me to beat Jelly he made that statement once
